literal: At the beginning of Huangshi, Xian submitted at Jingxing.
idiomatic: Early in the Huangshi era, Xian came in and submitted at Jingxing.

literal: Daowu asked Xian, "Of what state are you a subject?"
idiomatic: Emperor Daowu asked Xian, "What state do you serve?"

literal: What offices did your grandfather and you yourself hold?"
idiomatic: "What offices did your grandfather hold, and what have you yourself held?"

literal: Xian said, "Your servant is originally from Pingji in Zhao Commandery.
idiomatic: Xian said, "Your servant is a man of Pingji in Zhao Commandery.

literal: My great-grandfather Chong was Jin's Administrator of Pingyang and Right Marshal of the Grand General.
idiomatic: My great-grandfather Chong served Jin as Administrator of Pingyang and as Right Marshal to the Grand General.

literal: My father Mao was Shile's Administrator of Le'an and Left Commandant of the Center.
idiomatic: My father Mao held Shile's post of Administrator of Le'an and served as Left Commandant of the Center.

literal: Your servant was Fu Pi's Left Master of Guests, Murong Yong's Director of the Secretariat, and Marquis of Gaomi."
idiomatic: As for myself, I was Fu Pi's Left Master of Guests, Murong Yong's Director of the Secretariat, and Marquis of Gaomi."

literal: When the imperial carriage returned to Dai, Xian was made Right Gentleman of the Central Guard in the Secretariat.
idiomatic: When the imperial carriage returned to Dai, Xian was appointed Right Gentleman of the Central Guard in the Secretariat.

literal: He was again promoted to Erudite and Grand Rectifier of Ding Province.
idiomatic: He was promoted again to Erudite and Grand Rectifier of Ding Province.

literal: The emperor asked Xian, "What is best and can augment a ruler's wisdom?"
idiomatic: The emperor asked Xian, "What is the finest thing for sharpening a ruler's mind?"

literal: Xian said, "Only the classics—the governmental canons of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors—can supplement a king's wisdom."
idiomatic: Xian said, "Only the classics—the governmental canons of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors—can truly supplement a king's wisdom."

literal: He also asked, "I wish to gather the books of the realm—how should I proceed?"
idiomatic: He asked again, "I wish to collect all the books in the empire—how should I go about it?"

literal: He answered, "What the lord favors is not hard to assemble."
idiomatic: He answered, "Whatever the lord favors is not hard to bring together."

literal: The emperor thereupon issued orders throughout the realm, and the classics gradually accumulated.
idiomatic: The emperor then issued orders throughout the realm, and the canonical texts gradually piled up.

literal: When Daowu attacked Yao Xing at Chaibi he sought Xian's counsel.
idiomatic: When Daowu attacked Yao Xing at Chaibi, he sought Xian's counsel.

literal: Xian answered, "In war the orthodox joins battle; victory comes through the unexpected."
idiomatic: Xian answered, "In war one meets the enemy in the orthodox way; victory comes by the unexpected."

literal: I hear Yao Xing intends to encamp at Tiandu and profit from his grain route.
idiomatic: "I hear Yao Xing plans to encamp at Tiandu and exploit his supply line."

literal: Before he arrives, send a surprise force first to block Tiandu; set ambushes strictly on both sides of Chaibi to guard inner and outer approaches—if Xing wishes to advance he cannot, if he halts he lacks grain.
idiomatic: "Before he arrives, send a surprise force to cut him off at Tiandu first. Set ambushes firmly on both flanks of Chaibi to cover inner and outer approaches—if Xing tries to advance he cannot, and if he halts he will run short of grain."

literal: The high are roosts for the enemy; the deep are prisons for the enemy—what military treatises forbid.
idiomatic: "High ground becomes a perch for the enemy; deep ground a prison—exactly what the military treatises forbid."

literal: Yet Xing occupies such ground—he can be taken without fighting."
idiomatic: "Yet Xing has chosen such ground—he can be taken without a battle."

literal: The emperor followed his plan; Xing was indeed defeated and fled home.
idiomatic: The emperor followed his advice; Xing was indeed beaten and fled home.

literal: When Mingyuan acceded he asked his attendants, "Among the old ministers whom did the late emperor trust most?"
idiomatic: When Mingyuan took the throne he asked his attendants, "Among the old ministers, whom did the late emperor trust most?"

literal: Duke of Xinxin Wang Luo'er said, "There is Li Xian, whom the late emperor knew well."
idiomatic: The Duke of Xinxin, Wang Luo'er, said, "There is Li Xian—the late emperor knew him well."

literal: Soon Xian was summoned and read twenty-two chapters of Han Fei's Linked Pearls Discourse and eleven items of Taigong's Art of War.
idiomatic: Before long Xian was summoned in and read twenty-two chapters of Han Fei's Linked Pearls Discourse and eleven passages from Taigong's Art of War.

literal: An edict to the relevant offices said, "What Xian knows concerns great matters of army and state; from now on let him always lodge within the palace."
idiomatic: An edict to the relevant offices ran, "What Xian knows touches the great affairs of army and state; henceforth let him lodge always within the inner palace."

literal: Xian was granted silk brocade and an imperial horse, made General Who Pacifies the East and Marquis of Shouchun, and given twenty-two dependent households.
idiomatic: He was given silk brocade and an imperial horse, appointed General Who Pacifies the East and Marquis of Shouchun, and granted twenty-two dependent households.

literal: He died as Grand Director of the Inner Court at age ninety-five.
idiomatic: He died in office as Grand Director of the Inner Court, aged ninety-five.

literal: An edict granted him one suit of gold-threaded life-robes; he was posthumously made Governor of Dingzhou and Duke of Zhongshan, with the posthumous name Wengong.
idiomatic: By edict he received one suit of gold-threaded life-robes; posthumously he was made Governor of Dingzhou and Duke of Zhongshan, with the posthumous name Wengong.

literal: His son Guo inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Guo inherited the title.

literal: Guo's son Feng was an Erudite of the Secretariat.
idiomatic: Guo's son Feng was an Erudite of the Secretariat.

literal: Feng's son Yu, styled Yuankai.
idiomatic: Feng's son Yu, styled Yuankai.

literal: At the beginning of Taihe he successively served as Director of the Secretariat, Friend to the Prince of Qi Commandery, and Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West, concurrently Administrator of Fufeng.
idiomatic: Early in the Taihe era he served in succession as Director of the Secretariat, Friend to the Prince of Qi Commandery, and Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West, with concurrent appointment as Administrator of Fufeng.

literal: When the staff was dissolved he left the commandery post and settled in Chang'an.
idiomatic: When the princely staff was disbanded he relinquished the commandery post and made his home in Chang'an.

literal: Admiring the ancient method of eating jade, he went to gather it at Lantian, digging in person, and obtained more than a hundred pieces shaped like rings, disks, and miscellaneous vessels.
idiomatic: Enamored of the ancient practice of eating jade, he went to Lantian to gather it, digging with his own hands, and brought back more than a hundred pieces shaped like rings, disks, and other vessels.

literal: Some were rather coarse and black; he boxed them and brought them back all the same.
idiomatic: Some were rather coarse and blackish; he packed them in a box and carried them home anyway.

literal: When he looked at them at home, all were lustrous and pleasing.
idiomatic: When he examined them at home, every piece was lustrous and delightful to handle.

literal: Yu then pounded seventy pieces into powder and ate them, giving most of the rest away.
idiomatic: Yu then pulverized seventy pieces and swallowed the powder, giving away most of the rest.

literal: Later Yu and others who heard of it searched again at the old spot and found nothing.
idiomatic: Later Yu and others who heard the story searched again at the old site but found nothing more.

literal: The younger brother of Duke of Fufeng Yuan Huai obtained the jade, carved it into vessels and ornaments—all bright and precious.
idiomatic: The younger brother of Duke of Fufeng Yuan Huai acquired the jade and carved it into vessels and personal ornaments, all of them bright enough to be treasured.

literal: Yu took it for more than a year and said it had effect.
idiomatic: Yu consumed it for more than a year and maintained that it worked.

literal: But worldly affairs gradually encroached on his meals—he observed no restraint—and heavy drinking further harmed his will.
idiomatic: But everyday cares gradually crowded out his meals—he kept no discipline at table—and heavy drinking further dulled his spirit.

literal: When his illness grew grave he told his wife, "I never gave up wine and women and brought myself to death—it is not the medicine's fault.
idiomatic: As his illness worsened he told his wife, "I never gave up wine and women and have brought myself to this end—it is not the jade's fault.

literal: Yet my corpse will surely show something strange; do not bury me hastily, so that later men may know the marvel of eating jade."
idiomatic: Still, my corpse is sure to show something out of the ordinary; do not bury me in haste, so that men of later times may see the wonder of eating jade."

literal: It was mid-seventh month; Chang'an was fiercely hot, yet Yu's body lay four nights and its color did not change.
idiomatic: It was the height of the seventh month; Chang'an sweltered, yet Yu's body lay out four nights without its color changing.

literal: His wife Lady Chang placed two jade beads in his mouth as burial pebbles; his mouth closed.
idiomatic: His wife Lady Chang placed two jade beads in his mouth as funerary pebbles; his lips closed.

literal: Chang said to him, "You yourself said eating jade had divine proof—why not accept the pebbles?"
idiomatic: Lady Chang said to him, "You yourself claimed that eating jade worked miracles—why not take the pebbles?"

literal: When she finished speaking the teeth opened and admitted the beads.
idiomatic: No sooner had she spoken than his teeth parted and the beads went in.

literal: She breathed on his mouth; there was no foul odor at all.
idiomatic: She breathed close to his mouth; there was not the slightest foul smell.

literal: When they placed him in the coffin he lay straight and did not slump.
idiomatic: When they laid him in the coffin his body remained upright and did not collapse.

literal: At death he left several sheng of jade powder in a bag, put into the coffin.
idiomatic: At his death he left several sheng of jade powder in a bag, which was placed in the coffin with him.

literal: Xian's younger son Jiao.
idiomatic: Xian's younger son Jiao.

literal: In Tianxing, Daowu secretly asked Xian, "Will our descendants forever serve Wei as ministers, or will they serve another surname?"
idiomatic: In the Tianxing era Daowu asked Xian in private, "Will our descendants always remain ministers of Wei, or will they serve another house?"

literal: Xian said, "The state's government and transformation extend far—they cannot be reckoned to an end."
idiomatic: Xian said, "The state's governance and transforming influence stretch far into the future—they cannot be traced to an end."

literal: Jiao became a disciple of Kou Qianzhi and then for decades consumed qi and abstained from grain, living in seclusion on Mount Heng.
idiomatic: Jiao became a disciple of Kou Qianzhi and for decades thereafter fed on qi and abstained from grain, living in seclusion on Mount Heng.

literal: Past ninety, his face was like a youth's.
idiomatic: Past ninety, his face was like a youth's.

literal: One day he bathed, donned cap and belt; his family thought it strange, and soon he sat and died.
idiomatic: One day he bathed, put on cap and sash; his household found it odd, and presently he sat upright and died.

literal: Daoists all called it attaining corpse dissolution and the immortal way.
idiomatic: Daoists everywhere pronounced that he had achieved corpse dissolution and entered the immortal path.

literal: Jiao's grandson Yihui.
idiomatic: Jiao's grandson Yihui.

literal: In the Taihe era, for broad mastery of Confucian learning and literary talent he was made Recorder to Prince Qinghe Yi.
idiomatic: In the Taihe period, recognized for broad learning in the Confucian classics and for literary gifts, he was made Recorder to Prince Qinghe Yi.

literal: In memorials, letters, and memorials of state his prose needed no revision—clear, canonical, ample, and swift; his age praised him.
idiomatic: In official memorials, letters, and submissions his writing needed no polish—lucid, canonical, ample, and swift—and men of his day acclaimed him.

literal: He also compiled for Yi the Territorial Map and the Record of Manifest Loyalty.
idiomatic: For Yi he also drew up the Territorial Map and the Record of Manifest Loyalty.

literal: By nature he loved Laozi and Zhuangzi and greatly scorned Buddhism.
idiomatic: By temperament he delighted in Laozi and Zhuangzi and held Buddhism in contempt.

literal: When Empress Ling ruled, a monk Huilian charmed water for people to drink, claiming it cured illness; the common folk flocked to him by the thousands daily.
idiomatic: During Empress Ling's regency a monk named Huilian gave people water he had "charmed," claiming it cured disease; commoners rushed to him by the thousands each day.

literal: Yihui reported to Yi that this was sorcery and delusion.
idiomatic: Yihui reported to Yi that the affair was fraud and delusion.

literal: Yi had Yihui draft a memorial of remonstrance; the empress dowager accepted his words.
idiomatic: Yi had Yihui compose a remonstrance for the throne; the empress dowager took his advice.

literal: Yuan Cha hated Yi and transferred Yihui to Commissioner of the Metropolitan Waterworks.
idiomatic: Yuan Cha, who hated Yi, had Yihui transferred to Commissioner of the Metropolitan Waterworks.

literal: Soon Yi was killed; Yihui therefore abandoned office and lived in seclusion on Mount Dafang.
idiomatic: Before long Yi was killed; Yihui thereupon resigned his post and went into hiding on Mount Dafang.

literal: The younger son Lan was famed for pure filial piety and would not accept summons to office.
idiomatic: His younger son Lan won renown for unstinting filial devotion and would not answer summons to office.

literal: In Xiaochang an edict honored his gate and lane.
idiomatic: In Xiaochang an edict honored his gate and lane.

literal: In Zhengguang Prince Wensuan Dan succeeded; remembering Yihui's elegant integrity and steadfast loyalty, he recommended his grandson Jingru, who reached Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.
idiomatic: In the Zhengguang era, when Prince Wensuan Dan succeeded, he recalled Yihui's refined integrity and firm loyalty and recommended his grandson Jingru, who rose to Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.

literal: From Huangshi until Qi received the abdication—one hundred fifty years.
idiomatic: From the Huangshi era until Qi received the abdication was a span of one hundred fifty years.

literal: What Xian said had clear proof.
idiomatic: What Xian said had clear proof.

literal: Jingru's son Zhaohui ranged widely through antiquity, free and unbound; people of the time called him Gentleman Bo.
idiomatic: Jingru's son Zhaohui ranged widely through antiquity, careless of convention; contemporaries called him "Gentleman Bo."

literal: He was known by his style in Yan and Zhao.
idiomatic: He was known by his style in Yan and Zhao.

literal: Skilled in discourse, with grand eloquence; in writing he followed his own spirit and did not keep to ordinary rules.
idiomatic: He was skilled in debate and possessed sweeping eloquence; in composition he followed his own bent and ignored ordinary rules.

literal: His ambition favored reclusion; he admired Ge Hong's way of life.
idiomatic: He aspired to the life of a recluse and took Ge Hong as his model.

literal: Seeking teachers and the Way he traveled a thousand li without hesitation.
idiomatic: In pursuit of teachers and the Way he would travel a thousand li without flinching.

literal: Meeting the lofty he inclined his carriage-roof as to an old friend; meeting mediocrity he looked down even on kings and dukes.
idiomatic: Toward the truly lofty he would tilt his carriage awning as to an old acquaintance; toward the mediocre he would look away even from kings and dukes.

literal: At first he was a Daoist priest; in mid-life he answered the imperial summons and became Wei of Gaotang.
idiomatic: He began as a Daoist priest; in middle age he answered the imperial call and was appointed magistrate of Gaotang.

literal: In the Daye era he took wife and children into seclusion on Mount Song, styling himself Master Yellow Cap.
idiomatic: During the Daye reign he withdrew with wife and children to Mount Song, taking the sobriquet Master Yellow Cap.

literal: He had a collected works in ten scrolls, praised by scholars.
idiomatic: He left a collected works in ten scrolls, admired by scholars.

literal: Jia Yi, styled Yanlun, was originally of Guzang in Wuwei.
idiomatic: Jia Yi, styled Yanlun, was a native of Guzang in Wuwei.

literal: His sixth-generation ancestor Fu was Wei's Governor of You Province and Marquis of Guangchuan at Douting; the family settled there.
idiomatic: His sixth-generation forebear Fu had been Governor of You Province for Wei and Marquis of Guangchuan at Douting; the family made its home there.

literal: His father was Fu Jian's Administrator of Julu and was imprisoned for slander.
idiomatic: His father served Fu Jian as Administrator of Julu and was imprisoned for speaking ill of the throne.

literal: Yi at age ten went to Chang'an to plead his father's case and won release.
idiomatic: At ten Yi went to Chang'an to plead his father's case and secured his release.

literal: Near and far marveled, all saying, "This boy is splendid—a descendant of Jia Yi, none to match in the capital."
idiomatic: People near and far marveled, saying with one voice, "This boy shines like a star—a true descendant of Jia Yi, with none in the capital to equal him."

literal: At weak cap he was Agricultural Recorder to Murong Chui's Prince of Liaoxi.
idiomatic: At his coming of age he became Agricultural Recorder on the staff of Murong Chui's Prince of Liaoxi.

literal: Daowu had long heard his name and often sent envoys to request Yi from Chui; Chui only increased his respect.
idiomatic: Daowu had long known his reputation and often sent messengers to ask Chui for Yi; Chui only treated him with greater regard.

literal: Chui sent his heir Bao to raid; at Canhe they were utterly defeated—Yi and his cousin Run, Administrator of Dai Commandery, were captured.
idiomatic: Chui sent his heir Bao on a raid; at Canhe they suffered utter defeat, and Yi together with his cousin Run, Administrator of Dai Commandery, were taken prisoner.

literal: When Daowu acceded he was made Left Assistant Director of the Secretariat and took part in state affairs.
idiomatic: When Daowu took the throne he was appointed Left Assistant Director of the Secretariat and took part in governing the realm.

literal: At the end of Tianci, Yi asked to go to Wenyang to treat illness and was seized by rebel Hu and delivered to Yao Xing.
idiomatic: Near the end of the Tianci era Yi asked leave to seek treatment at Wenyang, was seized by rebel Hu bands, and sent on to Yao Xing.

literal: After several years he escaped home, was again seized by Helian Qubing, made Director of the Secretariat, and died.
idiomatic: After several years he slipped away and returned home, only to be seized again by Helian Qubing, who made him Director of the Secretariat before he died.

literal: When Taiwu pacified Helian Chang, his son Xiu met the coffin and buried him south of Dai.
idiomatic: When Taiwu pacified Helian Chang, his son Xiu went to meet the coffin and buried him south of Dai.

literal: Xiu was Junior Mentor to the Heir Apparent, enfeoffed as Baron of Yangdu, and Grand Rectifier of his native province.
idiomatic: Xiu served as Junior Mentor to the Heir Apparent, was enfeoffed Baron of Yangdu, and held the post of Grand Rectifier of his home province.

literal: When Xianwen acceded he was advanced to Baron of Yangdu.
idiomatic: When Xianwen acceded, Xiu's title was raised to Baron of Yangdu.

literal: At the time Chancellor Yi Hun's wife was of common birth yet sought the title of princess; she spoke of it repeatedly to Xiu, who remained silent.
idiomatic: At that time the chancellor Yi Hun's wife, though of humble birth, repeatedly pressed Xiu for the title of princess; Xiu would not answer.

literal: Later on public business he visited Hun at his residence.
idiomatic: Later, on a matter of official business, he called at Hun's private residence.

literal: Hun and his wife sat together and said harshly, "You oversee duties—nothing should be refused.
idiomatic: Hun and his wife received him together and spoke harshly: "You administer affairs of state—there should be nothing you refuse us.

literal: I ask for princess and you do not agree—what do you mean?"
idiomatic: I ask for the rank of princess and you withhold your consent—what is your meaning?"

literal: Xiu answered boldly, "The title princess, the designation king's daughter—the utmost of honor—is not fitting for a common clan."
idiomatic: Xiu replied with spirit: "The title of princess, the designation of a king's daughter—the summit of favor—is not for a clan of common birth."
